nutshell: Universal Multimodal Embeddings (UMEs) unify modalities/tasks into one embedding space but largely ignore visual identity discrimination (VisID) - recognizing that two images share the same specific identity. This paper formalizes VisID into four meta-tasks (Identity Recognition, Re-Identification, Identity Grounding, Identity Editing), introduces the MVEB benchmark (28 datasets, 522K samples) to train/evaluate it, and proposes an identity-aware sampling + unified contrastive loss training framework (VisME) that adds strong VisID capability to UMEs without sacrificing general multimodal performance.
contributions: A formal unified definition of VisID as a multimodal (image, text) query-candidate matching problem, decomposed into four meta-tasks: Identity Recognition, Re-Identification, Identity Grounding, and Identity Editing.

MVEB (Multimodal Visual Identity Embedding Benchmark): 28 sub-datasets (20 in-domain training + 8 out-of-domain evaluation) spanning all four meta-tasks, built via a 3-step pipeline - relevance/quality screening, identity-aware long-tail resampling plus auxiliary-model hard-negative mining for AIGC data, and identity-aware train/eval splitting (no identity leaks across splits where feasible).

An offline identity-aware batch scheduling scheme that pre-generates the entire training batch stream so each identity appears at most once per batch (avoiding false-negative pairs that plague naive in-batch sampling on identity-centric data), combined with structured hard-negative sampling for datasets with predefined hard-case relationships.

A single unified contrastive loss applied identically to both semantic-alignment tasks (caption as positive) and identity-discrimination tasks (another view/edited variant as positive) - task specificity comes entirely from how training triplets are constructed, not from separate loss functions.

VisME models (Qwen2-VL/Qwen2.5-VL backbones, 2B-7B) achieve best-in-class results on both the general MMEB benchmark and the new identity-centric MVEB benchmark simultaneously, including an Identity Grounding capability the paper claims is absent in prior UMEs.
deficiencies: The paper's own ablation (Table 2) shows most of the ID-aware sampling gain comes from simply eliminating false-negative pairs (MVEB IND 64.3→76.2, +11.9 pts) with MMEB essentially unaffected, while the more novel 'structured hard-negative mining' component on top adds only a modest further +1.5 pts (76.2→77.7) - the more basic fix does most of the work despite both being presented as equally central contributions.

MVEB is built, curated, and evaluated entirely by the same team that also proposes and reports the winning model (VisME) on it, with no independent third-party evaluation; Step 1's 'manual verification of relevance to VisID tasks' and 'dataset-level quality assessment' criteria for including/excluding entire source datasets aren't specified in detail, making full reproducibility of the benchmark's composition hard to verify from the paper alone.

The MVEB out-of-domain split covers only 8 of 28 sub-datasets, and results are reported only as meta-task or aggregate averages (never per-dataset) - given the sub-datasets vary hugely in scale (e.g. GLDv2 subsampled to ~30K vs. Product1m at native scale), it's unclear whether the reported 74-78.8 MVEB averages are driven uniformly or by a handful of easier sub-datasets.

Dual-encoder baselines (CLIP, SigLIP2, LLM2CLIP) are evaluated under a modified protocol that strips text from all tasks except Identity Editing, while VLM-based UME baselines keep their full instruction text - this asymmetry means Table 1's 'dual-encoder vs. UME' comparison isn't a fully apples-to-apples evaluation of the same task formulation.
notable: Table 3's cross-training ablation shows training on MVEB-only or MMEB-only barely transfers to the other benchmark (e.g. MVEB-only training: 51.7 MMEB-IND vs. 71.4 when MMEB-trained) despite both being framed as compatible tasks under one unified loss - suggesting general multimodal alignment and identity discrimination sit in more orthogonal regions of representation space than the 'unified framework' framing implies, and joint training is necessary rather than just convenient. Also notable: the SigLIP2 dual-encoder baseline (no LLM backbone at all) beats most 2B-scale VLM-based UMEs specifically on Identity Recognition (73.1 vs. many models in the 40s-60s range), suggesting bigger MLLM-based UMEs don't automatically dominate simpler dual-encoder designs on every identity subtask.
